paragraphs: Friend, this one is heavy, and I'm not going to joke about the wrong done to Tamar. Here's what the passage shows us. Amnon's problem started before any of it happened, with a desire he fed instead of stopping. Then his friend Jonadab, a "very shrewd man" (2 Samuel 13:3), handed him a plan, and clever advice is not the same as good advice.

Now look at Tamar, because she is the one to remember. She said no, she said it should never be done in Israel, and she begged him to stop (2 Samuel 13:12-13). She did everything right, and the wrong was still done to her, and that was never her fault. When the Bible says Amnon was "stronger" (2 Samuel 13:14), it puts the blame where it belongs, on the one who used his strength to hurt her. And I think the way Amnon's "love" turned into hatred (2 Samuel 13:15) tells us what it was all along: it was never love.

The rest of the family let her down too, friend, and the passage doesn't hide it. Absalom told her to be quiet (2 Samuel 13:20), David was furious (2 Samuel 13:21), and Absalom stayed silent and hated (2 Samuel 13:22). Anger with no action, and silence with no justice, leave a wound open, and that's why this story keeps going. So here's what I want you to carry out of my bakery: listen to the hurting, speak up for the one who can't, and be careful about the advice you take and the desires you feed.
